title: Strategic solidarity: solidarity and self-interest in Scandinavian contributions to global Covid-19 vaccine equity.
paragraphs: At the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, the One Campaign urged Nordic leaders to capitalise on their reputations as “open-minded, fair, and dependable partners” to push for a “robust, coordinated international response to the Covid-19 pandemic” [ 1 ]. The campaign stressed the need for financial support for global vaccine equity through the newly established Access to Covid-19 Tools Accelerator (ACT-A), 1 promoted as “the only global, end-to-end solution to the pandemic” [ 2 ]. Advocates argued that “when these [Nordic] governments speak out on inequality or injustice, the world listens” [ 1 ].

The Nordic states largely lived up to this image. Norway and Sweden were among only three countries credited with meeting their ‘fair share’ of ACT-A financing in 2021, while Denmark, Finland and Iceland made substantial, if smaller, contributions. Norway also co-chaired the ACT-A Facilitation Council, which helped mobilise nearly 24 billion dollars for Covid-19 vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics between April 2020 and September 2022 [ 3 ]. These efforts were consistent with the Nordics’ (self-)identity as social democratic states committed to solidarity, humanitarianism, and equity [ 4 – 6 ]. They also drew on legacies of Danish and Norwegian WHO Directors-General Halfdan Mahler and Gro Harlem Brundtland [ 7 ], and on an enduring commitment to global health initiatives that have sustained the region’s reputation and self-understanding as “global good Samaritans” [ 8 ] and humanitarian superpowers [ 9 ].

At the same time, Nordic governments – like all wealthy countries – did everything they could to secure Covid-19 vaccines as quickly as possible to immunise their own populations [ 10 , 11 ]. In a market characterised by scarcity, these self-protective policies exacerbated already stark inequities in access to Covid-19 vaccines and directly undercut the very multilateral initiatives the Nordic countries supported in the name of global solidarity. In short, they gave with one hand and took with the other.

How can we make sense of this seeming policy incoherence and the tension between multilateral leadership of global solidarity efforts and self-interested participation in competitive vaccine procurement? What policy drivers contributed to shaping Nordic countries’ management of the trade-offs between global and national priorities during the Covid-19 pandemic, and which lessons arise for future crisis response?

Scholarship on global health security and global health diplomacy often draws a sharp dichotomy between global solidarity and national self-interests. From these perspectives, the global health architecture is seen as primarily serving the security interests of wealthy countries, at the expense of human security, solidarity, and global justice [ 12 – 14 ]. Contributions that appear solidaristic are understood to be primarily motivated by foreign policy aims beyond global public health equity, including the pursuit of national health security, geopolitical aims, or commercial interests [ 15 – 20 ].

These literatures usefully emphasise foreign policy interests in global policymaking but largely underplay the role of domestic factors in shaping how national governments contribute to multilateral crisis responses. In a major global health crisis such as Covid-19, public authorities committed to multilateral cooperation must also juggle multiple, sometimes contradictory demands from domestic constituencies, such as strong support for global solidarity alongside political obligations and pressure from public opinion to prioritise national self-interest. We contend that analyses of domestic policymaking in key donor countries, including the Nordics, are essential to grasp the complexities and nuances of the global pandemic response.

We argue that the concept of ‘strategic solidarity’ better captures the empirical reality of pandemic policymaking than a rigid solidarity/self-interest binary, by showing how multiple domestic interests and foreign affairs policy priorities intertwine. The term may seem oxymoronic if we adopt purist definitions of solidarity – for example as a voluntary willingness to assist those perceived to share a social, cultural or political bond [ 21 ]; as a contractual obligation of membership in a political community; or as discretionary, merit‑based action [ 21 ]. In practice, however, solidarity and self-interest can be contingent and co-constitutive.

We propose that strategic solidarity can be understood both as a policy orientation expressed through institutional practices that are distinct from mainly security-driven logics emphasised in the global health security literature and as a justificatory frame used to manage public opinion and preserve national self-understanding in the face of apparent policy incoherence, particularly in solidarity-oriented states such as the Nordics.

We explore these dynamics through an in-depth study of how public authorities in Norway and Denmark – two Scandinavian Nordic countries – contributed to multilateral initiatives and diplomatic efforts to advance global vaccine equity during the acute phase of the Covid-19 pandemic (2020–2022). We explore how they managed tensions between global solidarity and national self-interest, and how they mobilised solidarity as a justificatory frame and strategic resource to achieve broader political objectives, through in-depth analysis of three policy debates (1): efforts to accelerate research and development of Covid-19 vaccines (2); financial and in-kind contributions to global vaccine distribution mechanisms, notably ACT’s vaccine pillar COVAX; and (3) positions on intellectual property (IP) reforms intended to scale up global vaccine manufacturing to improve global supply.

Across these policy debates, we show that domestic political pressures, public opinion, national identity, partisan dynamics and inter-ministerial tensions (e.g., between health vs foreign affairs) shaped how public authorities conducted multi-level diplomacy and balanced timely domestic vaccine access against support for collective pooled procurement mechanisms at global and European levels. Such factors are often under‑examined in global health diplomacy literature, which tends to focus on inter‑state negotiations and great‑power vaccine diplomacy [ 22 – 27 ]. While scholars have analysed the European Union (EU) response and national inquiries into vaccine strategy, this is, to our knowledge, the first study to interrogate how the smaller Nordic powers managed simultaneous commitments to multilateralism and national protection.

In conclusion, we show how both Norway and Denmark moved in and out of multilateralism on strategically flexible terms during the pandemic, and how understanding this behaviour can inform ongoing policy debates and help guide the design of future multilateral mechanisms that are better able to support genuinely equitable responses in future global health crises.

To explain why health has expanded into foreign policy agendas, Ruckert et al. [ 28 ] propose a methodological approach that focuses on three dimensions: features of institutions and the interest they represent in global health diplomacy; the ideational environment in which global health diplomacy operates; and issue characteristics of the specific health concern entering foreign policy. We used this framework as a heuristic device to identify key dimensions shaping the intersection of global and national vaccine policy and diplomacy.

We conducted in-depth qualitative policy analysis of Norway and Denmark’s contributions to the global vaccine response during the acute phase of the pandemic (2020–2022). In both countries, we reviewed publicly available material, including governmental and parliamentary archives, news articles, interviews, debates, and documents from civil society organisations and other relevant global-level actors (e.g. WHO, UNICEF, CEPI, CEPI – participants in ACT-A’s vaccine pillar COVAX) – and the European Commission (EC). Within these institutions, we identified key individuals (ministers, senior officials, civil society representatives) and scrutinised their statements and positions in press releases, social media and interviews.

In the Norwegian case, we further used material from the national Coronavirus Commission, including publicly available transcripts of 34 interviews with high-level officials central to Norway’s pandemic response [ 29 , 30 ], such as the Prime Minister, Ministers of Health and Development, other prominent politicians, and senior bureaucrats. We also draw on 10 interviews we conducted with Norwegian public servants involved in ACT-A during 2020–2022 as part of an earlier study on Norway’s global health engagement (used as background material only). As Denmark did not commission an official enquiry touching upon its global response and vaccine procurement, official material was more scattered across government. For Denmark, we conducted 12 qualitative interviews in 2024–2025 with central figures in the Danish pandemic response, including 2 ministers, 3 parliamentarians and 7 high-level civil servants from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Denmark and Statens Serum Institut.

We also conducted a media analysis in both countries to assess how their contributions to global vaccine efforts were framed, justified and communicated to the public. In Norway, we used the online news media archive Retriever/Atekst to retrieve and review all news articles ( n = 530) mentioning the term “COVAX” between 1 January 2020 and 1 December 2024 in six national news media outlets ( Aftenposten, VG, NRK, Dagbladet, Klassekampen, and Morgenbladet ). In Denmark, we systematically surveyed the media database Infomedia for articles across all Danish media mentioning “COVAX” during the same period ( n = 280).

Research assistants conducted a preliminary thematic analysis of transcripts and documents using NVivo and other software. All authors then collectively analysed emerging themes during residential workshops in August 2024 and May 2025. We triangulated interview data with policy documents and media findings to create a timeline of key policy debates and interpret our results. Given the political sensitivity of the topic, we prioritised publicly available statements in the media and interviews from the Norwegian Coronavirus Commission over direct quotations from confidential interviews. We have translated direct quotes from Norwegian and Danish into English, and take responsibility for any errors. All interviewees gave informed consent.

While this article focuses on three core policy debates on vaccine R&D, global distribution and IP reform, elsewhere we provide more detailed empirical accounts of Danish and Norwegian vaccine strategies, including how international and domestic politics shaped national procurement and contributions to international distribution [ 10 , 11 ].

A risk in examining a country’s self-perceptions and national identity is that researchers who are nationals of that country may inadvertently reproduce these narratives by taking them at face value. We seek to counter this by explicitly and critically interrogating Nordics self-narratives, drawing on our insider-outsider status (through international backgrounds and dual nationalities), by juxtaposing two national examples, and by incorporating feedback from international colleagues involved in the broader large research project from which this article derives.

The study has several limitations. First, the primary sources were produced under conditions of high uncertainty, with frequent revisions in a rapidly changing media and policy environment. To mitigate this, we triangulated information across multiple sources and included our own observations from the pandemic’s early phase. Second, cross-country comparison is challenging in some domains, particularly for financial contributions and vaccine donations, because records often lack clarity on what donations and contributions entail. For comparative analysis of financial contributions to the global response, we therefor relied primarily on the ACT-A Commitment Tracker.

Norway and Denmark’s financial support to boost R&D for Covid-19 vaccines in early 2020 provides a good illustration of how solidarity and strategic self-interest intertwined in the pandemic response. Policies to support vaccine R&D generally take the form of public subsidies to pharmaceutical companies and research institutions. The selection of recipients of these grants, and the conditions attached, determine whether they foster a global or more nationalistic approach. The Trump administration’s Operation Warp Speed, for instance, explicitly tied public R&D subsidies to domestic priority access as part of a large “America First” policy. By contrast, the Oslo-based global public-private partnership CEPI (Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations), which was a key ACT-A partner, included contractual clauses on equitable access in its R&D grants, notably preferential prices for low-income countries, and later during the pandemic, priority deliveries to the COVAX Facility [ 22 ].

In Denmark, our interviews suggest that the government considered supporting several organisations but ultimately focused its R&D funding on two key entities, with a clear emphasis on domestic support. In March 2020, Denmark made a relatively modest contribution of USD 1.45 million (DKK 10 million) to CEPI [ 31 ]. Subsequently, in August 2021, it committed USD 126 million (DKK 800 million) to its leading vaccine producer, Bavarian Nordic, to support the development of a new generation of Covid-19 vaccines [ 32 ]. As an EU member, it also indirectly supported R&D efforts funded by the European Commission.

In both cases, the Danish government justified its subsidies through a combination of self-interest and solidarity. Minister for Development Cooperation Rasmus Prehn noted that the contribution to CEPI would support “the development of vaccines that fortunately benefit everyone, including Danish citizens” [ 31 ]. Meanwhile the Minister for Health, Magnus Heunicke, emphasised that the support to Bavarian Nordic would strengthen national preparedness by “potentially securing Denmark’s access to a broader selection of vaccines and great supply security,” while also benefitting low-resource settings due to the relative ease of their distribution – unlike mRNA vaccines that demand ultracold storage in special freezers, these would only need regular refrigeration [ 33 ].

Norway, which unlike Denmark does not have a domestic vaccine industry, directed its R&D support entirely to CEPI. With a contribution of USD 292 million, Norway became CEPI’s third largest contributor during the pandemic, following Germany and the UK [ 3 ]. Moreover, CEPI emerged as the primary recipient of Norwegian support within the ACT-A initiative (Table 1 ). The Norwegian government took prompt action to provide early support to CEPI in February 2020. It also channelled funding through IFFIm, an ‘innovative financing mechanism’ set up by Gavi in 2006, which issues vaccine bonds on financial markets to frontload funding (i.e., make it immediately accessible in full). The government then repays these bonds with interests over a ten-year period [ 34 ]. These funding commitments reflected Norway’s ongoing commitment to CEPI, which it helped launch in 2017 and whose headquarters are in Oslo. Norway was CEPI’s largest funder prior to the pandemic, affording the country significant influence within the organisation [ 35 ] and Norway’s Global Health Ambassador during the pandemic, John Arne Røttingen, served as CEPI’s first CEO.

Norway contributed USD 727 million, ranking seventh among donors, with a ‘fair share’ score of 116%. Over two-third of the funding was allocated to vaccine development and distribution. With the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) as its largest recipient, Norway’s approach differed from the top ten contributors who mostly focused on Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, for vaccine procurement. By contrast, Denmark’s contributed USD 65.1 million to ACT-A, resulting in a ‘fair share’ score of only 15%, but this is contextualized by its indirect financing through the European Commission, which contributed significantly from the EU budget. Of Denmark’s direct contributions, half went to Gavi, while notable funding was also directed to WHO and UNICEF as COVAX’s delivery partner, with minimal support for ACT-A’s work on diagnostics and therapeutics

Senior officials overwhelmingly framed Norwegian investments in CEPI as an act of solidarity, and the media frequently highlighted the billions of Norwegian kroner given to underscore the country’s generosity and commitment to global cooperation [ 36 ]. According to the Minister for Development at the time, Dag-Inge Ulstein, Norway was “at the forefront of international efforts to increase access to vaccines” thanks to their investments and involvement in CEPI, COVAX, and EU vaccine procurement scheme [ 37 ]. Media coverage also emphasised CEPI’s equitable access requirements and its goal of ensuring that the entire global community benefit from a Covid-19 vaccine [ 38 ]. At the same time, officials emphasised that investing in CEPI directly served Norway’s interests. Then Minister of Health, Bent Høie, claimed that Norwegians would benefit from vaccines developed with CEPI’s support, and touted Norway’s “significant funding to CEPI” as part of the country’s “preparedness efforts” [ 39 ]. Media narratives underscored the benefits of hosting a leading vaccine organisation in Norway’s capital, reporting that CEPI’s CEO informed Norwegian authorities about the risks of a severe pandemic and shared information about promising vaccine technologies as early as January 2020. Later, in 2025, Norwegian authorities formalised access to CEPI’s expertise through a Memorandum of Understanding [ 40 ]. The Minister of Health remarked that the country’s endorsement of CEPI was a strategic asset in its negotiations with the EU to join its joint procurement agreement, granting Norway, as a non-EU member, “credibility” towards this ultimately successful effort [ 36 ].

Norway and Denmark’s contributions to multilateral initiatives for the collective procurement and global distribution of vaccines provide a second illustration of how officials sought to balance international solidarity with national self-interest, and the tensions that emerged. In June 2020, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance launched the COVAX Facility as part of ACT-A’s vaccine pillar COVAX. COVAX was established as a global procurement mechanism aimed at ensuring equitable access to Covid-19 vaccines for all countries, initially covering up to 20% of a country’s population. Wealthy countries had the option to pre-purchase vaccine doses for themselves and provide funding to subsidise the facility’s procurement of vaccines for low-income countries.

Norway and Denmark contributed USD 198 million and USD 29.2 million each to COVAX’s effort to procure doses for poor countries, with Denmark also contributing indirectly through the EU budget. Additionally, Norway opted to bolster COVAX by purchasing options for vaccine doses for its domestic use, intended to complement joint vaccine procurement through the EU [ 10 , 11 ]. This support must be understood in the context of the foundational and long-term contributions made by all three Scandinavian countries to the establishment of Gavi in 2000, which hosted the COVAX Facility. Notably Norway has been one of Gavi’s most committed donors, playing significant roles in its leadership and board. Gavi is often cited as a prime example of Norway’s dedication to saving lives globally [ 41 ].

Despite strong financial support from donors including Norway and Denmark, the COVAX Facility struggled to purchase vaccines. This was mainly due to wealthier countries securing superior access to limited vaccine supplies through various advance purchase agreements with pharmaceutical companies, which prioritised buyers in Europe and the US [ 42 ]. As a result, COVAX was consistently relegated to a lower priority in the vaccine distribution queue and eventually evolved into a hub for the sharing of wealthy countries’ excess vaccine doses [ 27 ]. Donations of excess doses became a crucial mechanism for wealthy countries, which faced rising allegations of being responsible for global vaccine inequity through their hoarding of doses [ 43 ]. Throughout the pandemic, the Norwegian government donated nearly 6 million doses through COVAX, while Denmark donated 10.78 million doses globally − 7.27 million through COVAX and 3.5 million through bilateral agreements [ 44 ].

In January 2021, the Norwegian government garnered significant international praise for its promise to share doses in parallel with the rollout of its national vaccination program. However, the first actual donation did not occur until July 2021, when most of Norway's population had already been vaccinated [ 45 ]. Similarly, the Danish government expressed its intention to donate vaccines by May 2021 [ 46 ], but did not do so until August 26 of that year [ 47 ]. Notably, both countries’ initial donations consisted of AstraZeneca vaccines that had been withdrawn from their national vaccination programmes in April and May 2021 due to safety concerns. Norway also donated 450,000 AstraZeneca doses procured through the EU joint procurement mechanism [ 48 ].

By this point in time, WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus had called on wealthy countries to immediately share vaccine doses, including by imposing a moratorium on third ‘booster doses’ until at least 10% of people in all countries had been vaccinated, noting that only two percent of Africans had received their first dose while wealthy countries were considering administering a third dose [ 49 ]. Norway’s response to this call illustrated the difficulties the government faced in balancing domestic vaccine distribution with international commitments. While an opinion poll commissioned by Norwegian People’s Aid indicated that three out of four Norwegians supported delaying booster doses to facilitate vaccine rollouts in countries with low vaccination rates [ 50 ], the government was under political pressure to maintain and expand its domestic rollout. Norwegian authorities ruled out postponing booster doses or diverting mRNA vaccines for international sharing. Moreover, instead of donating doses of the Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) vaccine when it was removed from the vaccination program, authorities chose to build a stockpile in case of future mRNA vaccine supply shortages [ 51 ].

In response, six civil society organisations published an open letter amid growing activism against ‘vaccine hoarding’ [ 52 ]. Facing dissent, Norway’s Minister of Health Bent Høie invoked Norway’s prior generosity, asserting that “if all countries in the world had done as much as Norway to provide vaccines to other countries, the situation would be different” [ 53 ]. He maintained that it is possible “to have two thoughts in your head at the same time,” pointing to the dual responsibilities of “protecting our own population and contributing to ensuring that everyone in other countries receives the vaccine” [ 53 ]. However, he did not acknowledge that the EU joint procurement scheme Norway relied on to vaccinate its own population had directly competed with COVAX for supplies, thereby contributing to the global disparities that were being decried.

Similarly, in Denmark the political sentiment was that donations would only be relevant once the country had “excess” vaccines. As the Minister for Health stated: “When at some point we will be in a situation where Danes will no longer need vaccines, we are free to do with excess vaccines, as we please,” reaffirming the importance of domestic vaccination needs, including boosters [ 54 ]. Even for opposition parties, the idea of heeding Tedros’s call to postpone boosters was politically untenable, with one politician referring to it as “political suicide” to “deprioritise Danes’ vaccine access” [ 55 ].

Nonetheless, the sale of 700.000 doses to New Zealand and Australia in the autumn of 2021 – justified by a political narrative of fiscal need – did spark a political stir. The left-wing party Enhedslisten criticised this decision, referencing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s statement during the UN General Assembly in New York 2020 where she “committed Denmark to vaccine solidarity” and argued for global access to vaccines [ 54 ]. Opposition politicians questioned the consistency of such a commitment with the government’s decision to sell vaccines to wealthy countries instead of donating them to African nations through COVAX. Heunicke, defended the sale, emphasising that sales rather than donations might benefit Denmark at a later stage: “There may also be situations where barter trades between Denmark and another country can provide access to other vaccine manufacturers. This could mean a faster vaccine rollout in Denmark, and we should not cut ourselves off from that” [ 54 ].

A key distinction between Norway and Denmark’s approaches to vaccine sharing was their preference for multilateral versus bilateral donations. Throughout the pandemic, Norway demonstrated a strong commitment to multilateralism by channelling its contributions almost exclusively through COVAX, which used a WHO-developed equitable allocation framework based on need. Occasionally, Norway shared vaccines through the EU when legal restrictions prevented COVAX from redirecting already shipped doses. 2 Unlike Norway, Denmark explicitly framed donations and vaccine diplomacy, particularly its bilateral parts, as extensions of Denmark’s broader geopolitical relationships, an approach that garnered bipartisan support across most of parliament. Denmark earmarked an early vaccine donation to North African countries and justified it on the grounds that “North Africa is an important neighbouring region to the EU” [ 47 , 56 ], utilising COVAX as a distribution mechanism while directly challenging its fair allocation principles [ 27 ].

Another illustration of linkage politics, where vaccine sharing was entangled with, and potentially leveraged to advance, other diplomatic objectives was Denmark’s attempt to donate 250,000 Johnson & Johnson vaccines to Rwanda announced in October 2021 following Danish officials’ visit to Kigali the previous month. This initiative, made outside both EU and COVAX frameworks, was seemingly not only motivated by needs – Rwanda had achieved a 13% vaccination coverage compared to neighbouring Uganda’s mere 1% – even if the country could theoretically also have been favoured for its stronger logistical readiness. Danish Development Minister Møller Mortensen characterised the donation as a “natural extension of our increased relations with Rwanda and the Memorandum of Understanding signed in the spring” [ 57 ]. These agreements were focused on establishing Danish-run asylum processing centres in Rwanda, a key element of the Social Democratic government’s 2018 campaign to deter asylum seekers from reaching Denmark by processing their claims in third countries. Ultimately, shortly before Christmas 2021, Rwanda declined the donation, a decision framed by Denmark as due to legal delays [ 58 ].

A third significant policy debate highlighting the tension between national self-interest and global solidarity concerned a proposal presented by India and South Africa to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in October 2020 to temporarily waive intellectual property (IP) rights for Covid-19 vaccines, drugs, and technologies. This “TRIPS waiver” proposal aimed to boost vaccine production in middle-income countries by shielding manufacturers from potential lawsuits over IP infringement and was widely framed as a measure of global solidarity [ 59 ].

Like other Western countries, as well as the EU, the Norwegian and Danish governments firmly opposed the TRIPS waiver. They presented two main arguments. First, they contended that a waiver was unnecessary because the TRIPS agreement already included flexibilities. They claimed that the main barrier to scaling up production was not IP but a lack of manufacturing capacity and weak health systems in developing countries. Second, they argued that a waiver could undermine the international innovation system and antagonise pharmaceutical companies [ 54 , 60 ].

This stance depoliticised the debate, positioning patent protection as a technical necessity instead of a political or ideological choice. Then Danish Minister for Health, Magnus Heunicke, emphasised the complexity of vaccine production [ 54 ]. Similarly, Norwegian Global Health Ambassador John-Arne Røttingen warned of potential harmful consequences for global and domestic interests, claiming that supporters of the waiver were engaging in “symbolic politics” ( symbolpolitikk ) which might harm the pharmaceutical industry’s incentives to develop and produce vaccines [ 61 ]. Then Norwegian Foreign Minister Ine Marie Eriksen Søreide criticised what she termed “experimental trade politics,” advocating instead for practical solutions that would yield more vaccines [ 62 ]. After Norway assumed the chair of the TRIPS council in March 2021 [ 63 ], Eriksen Søreide toned down Norway’s opposition, casting the country as a consensus-seeking broker among WTO member states [ 64 ].

Ironically, opposition to the TRIPS waiver was asserted in the name of solidarity. Government officials pointed to alternative policy solutions they deemed more efficient for promoting equitable access, such as COVAX and initiatives for voluntary licensing and technology transfer. Røttingen claimed that the TRIPS waiver was a distraction from pragmatic solutions. However, he was optimistic: “Fortunately, several of the [pharmaceutical] companies have said they will offer vaccines at cost price to low-income countries” [ 65 ]. Røttingen and Norway's then Minister of International Development, Dag-Inge Ulstein, jointly offered a set of voluntary “principles” rather than legal obligations for how the pharmaceutical sector could contribute to global vaccine equity, published by the World Economic Forum [ 66 ].

Norway became particularly active in promoting voluntary tech transfers as an alternative to IP reform. In May 2020, it became one of the few wealthy countries to endorse the WHO’s Covid-19 Technology Access Pool (C-TAP) – an initiative designed to facilitate technology transfer and voluntary licensing [ 67 ]. Additionally, the Oslo Medicines Initiative, launched in October 2020, aimed to ensure equitable access to high-priced medicines [ 68 ]. Although not focused on Covid tools, it signalled a political ambition to foster discussion about transparency in the pharmaceutical sector. Norway also contributed USD 40 million to the mRNA Technology Transfer Hub established in South Africa to boost research and manufacturing capacity in low- and middle-income countries [ 3 ]. However, these initiatives largely fell short. C-TAP received no backing from G7 nations and was even ridiculed by pharmaceutical companies [ 69 ]. The Oslo Medicines Initiative attracted scant interest and was phased out in 2022 [ 70 ], while the mRNA Technology Transfer hub did not complete its first technology transfer until September 2024 [ 71 ].

Despite these initiatives, Norway’s opposition to the TRIPS waiver jarred with its position as a leader in the global pandemic response, creating a contradiction that became more evident throughout 2021 as vaccine inequity grew and COVAX and other voluntary approaches failed to meet their goals. Civil society organisations like Norwegian People’s Aid and MSF, academics and health professionals, as well as leftist opposition parties ( Rødt and Sosialistisk venstreparti (SV)) were vocally critical [ 72 ]. Activist Erlend Grønning from the Norwegian branch of MSF argued that merely distributing vaccines is “old-fashioned” [ 73 ]. Left-leaning parties submitted two separate Private Members’ motions to the Norwegian parliament advocating for support of a more solidaristic international vaccine system, including support for the waiver, but both efforts were unsuccessful [ 74 , 75 ]. Then leader of the socialist party Rødt, Bjørnar Moxnes, called for Norway to use its role as Chair of the TRIPS council in the WTO to influence the patent waiver debate. In response, Minister of Development Ulstein did not address the TRIPS waiver directly, but asserted that Norway was working to ensure just pricing, increased production capacity and openness [ 76 ].

Norway’s position also attracted international outcry. The People’s Vaccine Alliance and MSF International explicitly singled out Norway as being among the small group of countries stalling progress in the discussion on a TRIPS waiver [ 77 ]. In an op-ed in Norwegian newspaper VG, Archbishop Thabo Makgoba of Cape Town challenged Norwegian Prime Minister Erna Solberg directly, asking, “How many more must die in India, Latin America, and Africa before she stops opposing poor countries’ efforts to produce more vaccines? There are no good reasons to withhold knowledge during a pandemic. It is ungodly, immoral, and a stain on humanity” [ 78 ].

In Denmark, the TRIPS waiver debate received less public scrutiny, with only a few politicians and civil society leaders calling for support. Leftist parties Enhedslisten and SF organised a debate in Parliament in January 2021 advocating for the waiver [ 79 ], but the motion was withdrawn ahead of a vote due to the government’s resistance. Subsequently, a coalition of Danish civil society organisations issued an open letter urging Prime Minister Frederiksen to support the TRIPS Waiver and demonstrate a “community spirit with the weakest and most vulnerable to Covid-19” [ 80 ].

In May 2021, President Joe Biden’s new administration in the US announced that it was changing the American position and would support waiving intellectual property protections for Covid-19 vaccines [ 81 ]. Norway’s Minister of International Development Ulstein was quick to celebrate the US’ position, taking indirect credit by highlighting Norway’s diplomatic engagement to find consensus: “As leaders in ACT-A and the TRIPS Council in WTO, Norway has worked to bring the parties together and find the necessary solution that everyone can agree on in order to ensure the production of as many vaccines as possible” [ 82 ]. Opposition politicians, however, derided the government for having failed to show leadership and for being a lackey to the US, calling Norway’s change of position a “panicked retreat” and embarrassing given the government had repeatedly voted against proposals equivalent to those now being celebrated. However, Minister of Foreign Affairs Søreide contended that “it is wrong that Norway has changed their stance on this matter [the TRIPS waiver]”. She claimed that Norway had been critical towards previous iterations of the proposed waver, but that Norway had been working towards a compromise from the beginning [ 82 ].

Finally, in June 2022, an agreement was reached during the WTO’s 12th ministerial conference, establishing a limited five-year waiver on Covid-19 vaccines, to be reviewed annually [ 83 ]. Decisions at the WTO are made by consensus, which means that neither Denmark nor Norway blocked the compromise. However, Denmark was much less supportive than Norway, which has been attributed in part to the important contribution of Denmark’s pharmaceutical sector to its total goods exports [ 84 ]. In any case, the agreed waiver was significantly narrower than the original proposal, limited to vaccine patents but excluding patents on diagnostics and therapeutics, as well as trade secrets, copyrights and industrial designs. The agreement also came so late that it had no bearing on the management of the acute phase of the Covid-19 pandemic.

This article has described how Norway and Denmark contributed to multilateral initiatives to advance global vaccine equity during the Covid-19 pandemic, constantly navigating between a commitment to global solidarity and national self-interest. Drawing on publicly available documents, media reports and interviews with key decision-makers, we examined their public funding for R&D to develop vaccines, their financial contributions to global vaccine distribution via COVAX, and their donation or sale of surplus vaccines. We also described their position on proposed reforms to ease IP protections to scale up vaccine production.

Our findings indicate that officials from both countries framed their contribution to the global vaccination efforts primarily in terms of solidarity, in line with Scandinavian countries’ traditional commitment to egalitarian and humanitarian values [ 9 ]. Both countries, and particularly Norway, did indeed commit significant financial resources and leadership to support equitable access. However, we argue that these enactments of solidarity were not purely altruistic; rather, they were strategically motivated too. Governments used newly established collaborative, multilateral initiatives to address shared challenges and to promote vaccination as a global public good, while simultaneously leveraging these efforts to advance their own foreign and public health policy interests and to manage domestic political pressures and public opinion during a major crisis.

Scholarship on global health security has often described global governance during pandemics as primarily serving the security interests of wealthy countries at the expense of human security, solidarity, and global justice [ 12 – 14 ]. This perspective views the global response to Covid-19 as a series of broken promises by affluent nations, leading to gross vaccine inequity and eroding trust in multilateralism [ 23 , 27 , 67 , 69 ]. While highlighting the structural roots of global inequities – which Steve Masiyiwa has called “a deliberate global architecture of unfairness” [ 85 ] – this view overlooks how individual countries and their domestic politics shape this global architecture. Efforts to rank countries’ financial contributions to multilateral initiatives like ACT-A in terms of their ‘fair share’ or other metrics similarly obscure the complexities behind wealthy nations’ policies; countries can both pay their fair share and at the same time undermine equity goals. This is a tension well-known outside global health too, such as in the debates surrounding tied aid and the donor self-interest of surface-level solidarity efforts [ 86 ].

Our approach acknowledges that these dynamics extend beyond a simplistic Global North versus Global South dichotomy. Dismissing the engagement of Western nations as purely nationalistic, neocolonial, or self-serving obscures a more nuanced understanding of self-interest and solidarity as contingent [ 87 , 88 ].

For example, we demonstrated how Norway and Denmark’s public subsidies for Covid-19 vaccine research and development blended self-interest with humanitarian motives. Norway, lacking a domestic vaccine industry, directed its support through CEPI, which prioritised equitable access for low-income countries. By supporting CEPI, Norway sought to promote global equity, but also to support a Norwegian-founded and hosted initiative while enhancing its diplomatic standing and securing benefits from future vaccine innovations. Likewise, Denmark, which made heavy R&D investments with the Danish company Bavarian Nordic, aimed to create vaccines suitable for distribution in low-income regions, while also ensuring broader access to multiple vaccine candidates for its citizens. This strategy also positioned its vaccine manufacturer competitively for post-Covid preparedness investments.

In both countries, financial contributions to COVAX were framed not only as humanitarian assistance but also as a strategic means to control the virus’s spread, protecting Norwegian and Danish citizens from the risks of dangerous mutations. While Denmark and Norway’s vaccine donations increased access for poor countries in the latter half of 2021, they were not merely a charitable act; these donations mitigated reputational risks associated with vaccine hoarding and allowed authorities to dispose of excess doses without facing accusations of wasting public funds. Norway’s preference for multilateral donations through COVAX ensured the equitable allocation of scarce doses, while also reinforcing its status as a global health leader and solidifying its reputation as a role model, helping to grant it access to high-level political fora like the G20. In contrast, Denmark’s bilateral donations and strategic earmarking for specific regions aimed to yield foreign policy gains, even though donating through COVAX would have been more cost-effective, efficient and better aligned with public health needs.

Norwegian and Danish officials deflected criticism about their opposition to the proposed TRIPS waiver by highlighting their generosity towards ACT-A and COVAX for the purchase of pandemic tools. While claiming that voluntary approaches served equitable vaccine access better than IP reform, their position revealed not just public health rationales but also self-interested motivations. Both nations preferred partnership over conflict with pharmaceutical companies, given their financial and reputational investments in market-based policies like the public-private partnerships CEPI and Gavi, which came together in ACT-A and COVAX, their reliance on these firms for their own Covid-19 supplies. Denmark also safeguarded the intellectual property interests of its growing pharmaceutical sector, highlighting how important commercial interests can be in influencing health policy [ 42 ].

Our analytical approach also emphasises that global health diplomacy operates across interconnected national, regional and global levels. As we demonstrate, solidarity operationalised at one policy level can either reinforce or undermine policies pursued at another and can be leveraged strategically in a multi-level game.

Dynamics similar to those we describe in Denmark and Norway also operated at the European level. Research on the EU’s Covid-19 vaccine policy shows that regional solidarity trumped unilateral, nationalistic responses within Europe, contributing to ensure equitable and simultaneous access for all EU and European Economic Area (EEA) member states (Norway, Iceland and Lichtenstein) [ 26 , 89 ]. In parallel, the European Commission assumed a prominent global leadership role by helping to establish ACT-A and contributing nearly a third of COVAX’s funding [ 90 – 93 ]. Initially, it did not perceive a contradiction between this global health leadership and EU-focused vaccine procurement. However, once vaccines became scarce and distributional conflicts intensified in late 2020, the Commission faced accusations of hoarding doses for Europeans and undermining COVAX’s supply [ 94 ]. Combined with its fierce opposition to a TRIPS waiver, this stance sat uneasily with its declared commitment to global solidarity [ 25 , 90 , 91 ].

We contribute to this scholarship by showing how Norway and Denmark’s global health policies were intertwined with those of the EU. Norway’s stated commitment to global solidarity and its established leadership in global health strengthened its position in negotiations over its own access to the EU joint vaccine procurement scheme, allowing it to benefit from European solidarity. At the same time, Norway’s status as a non-EU European country, despite its EEA membership, both enabled and constrained its global health policies [ 95 ]. On the one hand, its independence and reputation as a solidaristic and generous nation helped secure its nomination by the European Commission to co-lead ACT-A’s Facilitation Council and later to chair the WTO’s TRIPS Council, positioning it as bridge-builder between the EU and the global arena. On the other hand, its dependence on EU vaccine access limited its autonomy to operate on the global level and helps to explain its resistance to a domestic push to support the TRIPS waiver, instead aligning with the EU’s opposition.

In response to accusations of vaccine nationalism throughout 2021, the European Commission increasingly promoted a “Team Europe” approach [ 26 , 96 ], combining branding – highlighting the total contribution of EU institutions and member states – with efforts to coordinate and align different European countries’ global health policies [ 26 , 90 ]. Denmark’s global contributions were increasingly branded as part of “Team Europe” efforts, communicating its commitment to multilateral initiatives while still allowing more self-interested policies. For example, its decision to donate vaccine doses bilaterally reflected broader foreign policy objectives, including addressing domestic concerns around immigration through a strategically targeted vaccine donation offer to Rwanda.

Finally, our analysis underscores the importance of national identity, party politics and public opinion management in shaping multilateral responses – factors often overlooked in global health diplomacy scholarship that mainly focuses on inter-state relations.

In both countries, we found broad cross-party agreement and strong public support – in parliamentary debates, opinion polls and media coverage – for global solidarity as framed by COVAX and its twin mission: developing vaccines with equitable access conditions (through CEPI) and distributing them to countries with less access (through Gavi). In Norway, however, the government’s decision to allow third ‘booster’ doses in 2021 drew criticism for undermining global vaccine access, as reflected in media debates and the aforementioned poll for Norwegian People’s Aid showing that three in four respondents supported postponing boosters. At the same time, right-wing and centrist parties called for using COVAX-bound doses that had been purchased before Norway joined the EU joint procurement. These tensions highlight the political difficulties governments can face if global solidarity efforts delay or reduce the volume of the national vaccine roll-out, and the need to factor such dynamics into future preparedness efforts [ 10 , 11 ]. The main political conflict around global solidarity concerned the TRIPS waiver and challenges to industry monopolies, with civil society organisations and opposition socialist and communist parties in both countries challenging the government’s position and seeking to politicise the issue.

Our findings resonate with work on Scandinavia’s “humanitarian exceptionalism,” which shows how humanitarian values have long influenced the region’s international image and self-perception [ 95 , 97 ]. Policymakers have strategically leveraged this humanitarian brand to gain access, legitimacy and status on the global stage, and to foster identity-building and manage public opinion at home [ 9 ]. During the pandemic, Norwegian officials frequently invoked their country’s status as one of the most generous per capita donors in debates about global vaccine inequity. Minister of Health Bent Høie portrayed Norway’s solidarity as exceptional, claiming that global vaccine inequity would decline if other nations emulated Norway’s actions [ 98 ]. Senior officials framed Norway’s role as leading in an international dugnad , a concept that evokes voluntary collective effort for a common good [ 99 ]. Similarly, Danish officials drew on the notion of samfundssind , denoting shared societal responsibility.

We argue, however, that this narrative also deflected attention from the complicity of wealthy states – Denmark and Norway included – in deepening global vaccine inequality. Despite strong rhetorical support for COVAX and other global solidarity initiatives (in Norway more so than in Denmark), we observed little public backlash against the governments’ domestic vaccination procurement policies. Public debate focused instead on whether governments could have secured even more doses, faster. In Norway, the gap between the solidarity rhetoric and entrenched inequalities in access did not fundamentally challenge the country’s self-image as exceptionally generous: its status as a ‘humanitarian superpower’ remained largely intact both domestically and internationally. In Denmark, public and political debate, as we have shown, concentrated on pace and adequacy of domestic vaccine procurement, with global solidarity questions occupying a more marginal position. Christopher Browning’s argument that “being good” is so central to Scandinavian identity that challenges can feel like existential threats and thus are often unarticulated or dismissed [ 100 ] fits the Norwegian context particularly well. Our findings, and especially the Norwegian case, also support Kristian Bjørkdahl’s claim that expressions of outrage at injustice in Scandinavia can prompt a cathartic response of recommitment to humanitarian ideals, with promises ‘to do better next time,’ without critically interrogating the underlying structures and privileges that facilitated the failures in the first place [ 101 ].

The concept of strategic solidarity, as applied to Norwegian and Danish global health diplomacy during Covid-19, challenges a simple solidarity/self-interest binary. It demonstrates how these elements can be mutually reinforcing and interdependent, and how Scandinavian countries’ global health policies emerge from a multi-level interplay of national, regional and global politics. This interplay generates trade-offs and unintended consequences when objectives at different levels clash. It also highlights the significance of national identity, party politics and public opinion management. Although our examples are Nordic, the concept is not about Nordic exceptionalism: strategic solidarity alludes to the entanglements between drivers of action and inaction and between moral claims and strategic interest evident in initiatives such as China’s Health Silk Road and India’s Vaccine Maitri, despite the overtly bilateral nature of such initiatives.

Norway and Denmark’s experiences show how national strategic interests are continuously woven together with shared norms and aspirations in multilateral health engagements. This has implications for current debates about the need to reform multilateral institutional design [ 102 – 104 ] and for moving beyond traditional cooperative assumptions toward architectures capable of channelling competitive dynamics into positive-sum outcomes. While normative appeals are vital, they are insufficient to overcome the strategic, interest-based considerations embedded in multilateralism.

The findings also underscore the need for greater policy coherence amid the growing regionalisation of global health governance, which is leading to overlapping institutions, mandates, and authorities across multiple policy levels. As it becomes harder to conclude global agreements, regional cooperation grows more attractive, but can reinforce forum-shifting practices [ 105 ] and lead to contradictory and competing outcomes across levels. Our findings suggest that improving pandemic governance, and global health governance more broadly, requires not only better coordination, but also more systematic methodologies for understanding interdependencies and compromises among multilateral, regional and bilateral initiatives.

In a context of major aid cuts and the dismantling of multilateral institutions, framing policies in terms of “strategic solidarity” may help sustain public support for development aid by better anchoring them within public opinion, without dismissing the value of solidarity. Crucially, it may support a shift away from a charity-based model of aid towards one based on global public investments, in which collective action is directed towards tackling transnational problems and explicitly recognises that solidarity and self-interests are inherently intertwined in efforts to address global challenges [ 106 , 107 ].

ACT-A was established in April 2020 to support the development and equitable distribution of covid vaccines, diagnostics and treatments and facilitate coordination between ten global health organizations working on the issue. The vaccine pillar of ACT-A, known as COVAX, was co-led by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, the World Health Organisation (WHO), and the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI).
